reason: The judgment did require a rationally based section 3 opinion, but the quote is from another case and the statement omits the rational-basis and unauthorized-occupation qualifications.

The court adopted the no-right-to-revocation point where possession and public purpose remained, but the quote is from another case and the operative provisions were sections 39 and 39A rather than section 38.
The court quashed the acquisition steps because the objector's section 4 objections were not considered and no hearing opportunity was given.
The court only found a prima facie right in the nature of a servitude for the time being under Primary Court procedure, and the quote is borrowed authority rather than this court's holding.
The court did order exemplary costs for abusive litigation conduct, but the supporting quote is a quoted passage from another case.
The due-process proposition reflects the holding on the premature ex parte inquiry, but the quote is a foreign judicial-review quotation rather than the court's case-specific holding.
The court varied the shares because the plaintiff had admitted the fourth defendant's entitlement and possession, while the quote is only a factual pleading recital.
The court allowed appeal-stage submissions on title because of the Partition Act title-investigation duty, but it refused the fresh-evidence application and the quote does not support a retrial rule.
The court held that the pre-action deed tendered in evidence entitled the fourth defendant to the additional ten perches.
The judgment recognized exclusion of a wrongly included separate lot but expressly said the court has no power to declare the separate lot's owner in the interlocutory decree.
The court held that conversion of the strip into a roadway under the deed condition gave the plaintiff and predecessors or assigns the right to use it.
The court allowed the appeal because the plaintiff in rei vindication failed to prove the title pleaded and relied on.
The prescription rule was central to the decision, but the selected quote omits the starting-point requirement and appears in the court's discussion of earlier authority.
The court rejected the misjoinder objection and held that trust and unjust enrichment went together on the facts of the transaction.
The possessory-action rule under section 4 was applied, but the supporting quote is only an introductory fragment and does not state the rule.

The court did require the plaint to state whether the land was paraveni or acquired property, but the quote concerns omitted illegitimate children and the cited section is not the operative plaint provision.
The burden rule was applied against the defendant, but it is not a construction of Prescription Ordinance section 3.
The court set aside the decree because the trial judge had failed to identify the partition corpus and its boundaries before partitioning it.
The estoppel rule for a lessee or licensee was applied, but the selected quote is from an earlier case rather than this court's own holding.
The burden shifted to the defendant once paper title was proved, but the quote is from another case and Evidence Ordinance section 68 concerned proof of deeds, not this burden rule.
The court held that the defaulting purchaser was not a licensee but a trespasser who could not resist the plaintiff's title and ejectment claim.
The statement reverses the passage relied on, since the quoted submission said joinder could be done under section 36 and the court rejected the objection mainly because it was not raised below.
The court upheld the preliminary objection because defaulting defendants who filed no claim and obtained no leave under section 25 were not aggrieved parties for appeal.
The court applied the knowledge bar to laesio enormis, but the quote is from prior authority and Evidence Ordinance section 101 only concerned burden of proof.
The same-capacity and co-owner possession principles were applied, but the quote is from Corea and the statement omits the material ouster exception.
